background.speaker: [target]
background.text: First of all, I am thrilled to be here, and I'll try to answer everything as honestly as I can. Rates were going up. Rates going up is always a danger sign for a lot of people. Remember, they went from zero to two and then from two to five. The 10-year went from basically two to five. It shouldn't have been a surprise. I wasn't surprised. The Fed was surprised. They were telling you all that it was going to stay at 2%. And they were telling all the banks that, they were telling the world that, that rates were going to be low forever. And when they started going up, kind of Warren Buffett's quotes, when the tide goes out, you see who's swimming naked. And so you saw it in a bunch of things. It wasn't catastrophic. The only catastrophic was those two banks and another one called Signature. And they had, Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic had two things. One was known and one wasn't really known. One was this kind of, you talk about uninsured deposits, but this is more like uninsured deposits that were kind of like a flock, very concentrated. So it belonged to all the banks. It belonged to all the venture capital companies. So it was the thousand venture capital companies and their 30,000 constituent companies. So when the venture capital guys sent that email out, move your money, you know, all these people moved and also all the people that worked those companies. And so you literally had a Silicon Valley Bank, $100 billion move in a day. That was unique. Hadn't happened before. It's not the same as uninsured deposits, which is what some people think. And First Republic had essentially the same thing. I should point out, and the other, the second thing, which was known to everybody, any one of you can read a balance sheet. The balance sheet is the interest rate exposure that Silicon Valley Bank had. They'd invested a lot of their money in 3% mortgages, in HTM, health to maturity. The difference in health to maturity and affordable for sale is in health to maturity, not the market to market. But the world, I always tell people, forget the accounting. The market decides whether they think you're good or not. And what happened is their big portfolios lost a lot of value. And then when you said, what's the tangible book value of Silicon Valley Bank, if they had to market that to market, they'd lost, I forgot, 75% or 80%. And that kind of caused the run. This huge loss of debt, people run out. They hadn't pre-positioned collateral at the Fed, so they were unable to sell some of these bonds they had to their liquidity crisis. Government steps in. They stepped in very badly. They made a huge blunder, which I won't bore you with, which cost all of us $10 billion. Us, by the way, is the banks. FDIC is a mutual insurance company that the banks pay for. The government has never paid a penny. They've never paid a penny. It's cost us $20 billion in the last 10 years alone. So this kind of moral hazard of mismanagement by the FDIC. And then First Republic was in the same position. They let it go on for too long. We called up Secretary Yellen and whoever and said, we can handle it. And we went back and forth. And we ended up buying that. We didn't have to do it. We didn't necessarily do it. We did it to help the system. Obviously, it had some financial benefit for us. And you're going to see some new branches around here as we try to replicate some of the things that they actually did do very well. And of course, the second we bought it, you never heard about it again. We just sucked it in, managed it, hedged everything overnight. But it did take 10,000 people working a year to do it. And when you say the government bailing out, the government would have no idea how to do stuff like that. JP Morgan bailed them out. The other banks paid $10 billion to do it. And so that's what happened. And it does highlight, people then come up with all the reasons they should change rules and regulations. If I had been running the FDIC, I never would have allowed interest rate exposure. I never would have allowed interest rate exposure. I never would have allowed interest rate exposure. I never would have allowed interest rate exposure like that ever, sine qua non. The other stuff they might have missed, and there are other things you can be fixed about the discount window and how you have to pre-position collateral and some technical stuff, had nothing to do with capital per se. And it shouldn't happen. I mean, two little banks basically go bankrupt, and it's a whole big kerfuffle. We should have built a system that's more resilient than that, and it's not. So all this resolution recovery stuff, and basically, as I tell them, it doesn't work. So we should go back to the drawing board. Build a system. If the bank fails, it's not a big deal. And there are ways to do it. Some technical, some may take legislation that you have a banking system which doesn't have a problem that causes it for everybody.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_02
background.text: Let's talk a little bit more about that and what could give more resilience in the banking system. At the time, you mentioned sort of two key banks failed, but, you know, research by some of my colleagues here at the GSB suggested that, you know, there were hundreds of banks that were potentially in a similar position to Silicon Valley Bank and others in the sense of not managing their interest rate risk effectively, which calls some question into the regulations involved. But, you know, going back to that, first of all, you know, if the Fed had not stepped in to insure depositors and lend against the collateral they had,

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: The FDIC.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_02
background.text: Exactly. Do you think the problem has gone away? Have we recovered from that or is it sort of covered up and festering?

ground_truth: When we bought First Republic, we were quite probably said, this is the last domino unless rates go up. And so we do, what I know your academics did here, we have a heat map and we do bank by bank, name by name, what would happen if rates go to, I'm gonna say 6%. What would happen to the value of their real estate portfolios? What would happen if there was a recession? What would happen to their HTM? And so if that happened, a lot of banks would be in the red zone. So they were close to it, but not in it. Rates did not go up more than that, so they were kind of fine. But I still say, if rates go up and you have a recession, yeah, some will be in the red less. Some have been more responsible by raising capital, raising liquidity, being a little more careful, putting up reserves for commercial real estate. But if rates go to 6%, hey folks, a lot of stuff is in the red zone. And most people don't believe it's possible. It is possible. I'm prepared for 8%. JP World do fine at 8%. We don't run our company betting on interest rates. And so, but that, and that, if you had higher rates and higher credit spreads, certain private equity, certain private credit, there may be some insurance companies, it might be a bunch of banks. There are probably some things we don't even know about today that kind of comes out of the woodwork at that time. So yeah, that's what could cause a thing. But think of stagflation, recession, which most people don't even put it on their radar scope. And another very important point, the Feds, the CCAR test that people do is one test. And it's basically a great financial crisis test. It's a full of shit test. It doesn't work. It doesn't make a damn bit of difference. We do a hundred a week. If you think I care about their one test, but it lulls people to false sense of security. And so the regulators has been all the time in this other stuff, as opposed to maybe what they should have. So what I look at, which I think people should always do is, and I think it's a good intellectual exercise, particularly for students, lay out all the possibilities, whether you believe they're true or not. Can we have a recession with 0% rates again, a boom mark with 0% rates, a recession with 8% rates, stagflation. Can we have markets that actually go? Yeah, you can. And also think what would cause that? Because it makes you think a little bit harder about what are the factors, the future factors out there, not the past factors, which people focus on, but the future factors that could really affect this stuff. And that's called basic risk management. A lot of different what ifs and how can you handle it? And basically when you're a business, you want to be able to handle that regardless. So if we had 8% rates with the stagflation, JP Morgan would be fine. Our earnings would be down. I don't actually care about it. I don't care about that that much, but I can invest in the future. We can hire people. We can serve our clients. We don't have to pull back anywhere. So that is what I think they should be doing. And that's why I've always thought the C-Card thing was literally a complete misguided effort at risk management.

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: The capital is not the issue. I know that you have some professor who think, oh, 25%. We have 300 billion of equity capital and a trillion and two of loans.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_02
background.text: It is 25% of loans. We make $60 billion a year. Even the stress test has us losing money. We make money that year. It's not capital. There are other things which are, you know, cause problems. And by the way, there should be nothing wrong with banks going bankrupt. That's the normal system. They're trying different things. They're doing different things. They're merging different things. So you're not looking for fail-safe. You're looking for a system that's healthy construction, deconstruction or stuff like that. And so our system, I have a thing I put in my chairman's letter years ago called the spaghetti chart. We set up, not all Dodd-Frank was wrong. So I'm not arguing that. I'm not arguing that all regulation is wrong. But you gotta take a step back at this point. A Byzantine system. We set up multiple regulators. There are seven responsible for mortgages, five responsible for exchanges, three responsible for this. They can't even agree among each other what to do. So it literally cripples them. And then I look at this G-CIFI, which you probably don't know about. The calculation is completely asinine. CCAR doesn't work. Basel III was ill-constructed. And cutting across all that, resolution recovery is 80,000 pages long. It will never work. It's a complete waste of time. And so you have this system now. And what have they been doing for 10 years? Just adding more. Liquidity, LCR, G-CIFI, TLAC, this thing. So some of those things are good. But you associate it with yourself. What they missed was the opportunity to just take a step back and say, how do you build the best financial? We have the best in the world. So just keep that in mind. On that point. But they should have stepped back and said, what do we want? What do we want in the system? What do we want out of the system? How much resilience do we want? Do we want bankruptcies? Do we want more insurance? Do we want to favor small businesses? They never did any of it. Ever. Nothing. No cost-benefit study. No analysis. No expected outcomes. Zero.

ground_truth: Yeah, the world is not binary. There are all these flaws we have, and there are all these wonderful things about the country. You know, and I've given examples in the past where we grew at 2% a year for 20 years. And I think it should have been 3%. I think the reason it wasn't 3% is because we didn't get so many things right. Affordable housing, work skills, education, literally an overweening bureaucracy that just cripples the formation of business, etc. Had we grown at 3%, so 2% is not bad. I mean, if you're Europe, you would have loved 2%. But had we grown 3%, our GDP per person would have been 15,000 per person higher this year than it was. And that's a big number. That would have paid for a lot of benefits and services and growth and capital investment. And so I look at it sometimes, I look at, well, what are the policies that can drive that? What did we get wrong and what should we fix? And just because we're doing better than Europe doesn't mean we shouldn't be losing. A little more ambitious than what we think we're going to accomplish.

ground_truth: I think I mentioned the fiscal monetary stimulation and the effect of that and maybe persistent inflation and the geopolitics. I do believe it's the most complicated and risky geopolitical situation since major conflict. You have the ongoing conflict in eastern Europe. What's going on in the Middle Eastern region is terrible. You have one nation maybe on the verge of nuclear weapons, another sending troops. And we have a world that may be on fire, but it's smoldering. And leadership is required to fix this. And then we have the complexity of international relations. It's not just one region, but think of the global economic relationships. I just think those are really important subjects. I think we'll get through them. And we shall applaud anything we can do to get through those issues. But that is of great concern to me.
